149	
150	- `research/extracts/`: the POPL 2019 paper, Steele's talks of 2015 and 2016, and the project's web sites with the post of July 2012 that ended the project;
151	- the reading of the team's 2012 patents: `explorations/reviews/mie-probes/patents-forest-rule.md`.
152	
153	If a conflict or a decision not taken needs the designers' reason for a rule, print the row of its design area. WORD is a word of the area, such as `coercion`, `juxtaposition`, `dispatch` or `Arrays`. A word can match several rows, each about 1 to 2 KB.
154	
155	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#The map, by design area@WORD'
156	
157	Then open the sources that the row names. Among them are the `\note{}` boxes and the team's written rationale in the Internal Document appendix: `Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex` and `future.tex`. The row also names the later works that speak to its area, after the words "after the repository (§7)". To read what one of them covers and does not cover, print its row of the map's section "After the repository". WORD is a word of its title, such as `Polymorphic`, `patents`, `JuliaCon` or `Wrapping`. A row is about 1 to 2 KB.
158	
159	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#After the repository@WORD'
160	
161	When your report describes the team's sources on a question, say which of them is one of the late positions above. If the question is about a type rule, also name each later work that you checked.
162	
163	## The procedure
164	
165	1. Search the record with the queries in `records.md`. If two of the team's sources disagree, look for the construct in `revival-changes.md` before you search the record.
166	2. If the record or `revival-changes.md` settles the question, go back to building. Cite what settles it.
167	3. If you have evidence against a decision of the curator, read its POSITIONS entry and the notes that it names. If the decision used your evidence, go back to building.
168	4. Search the original tree. These help: the feature table and the phase map (`compiler.md`, "Before an edit"), the `\note{}` boxes and the map of design areas ("Weighing the sources" above), and the history of a file (`records.md`, "The repository's history").
169	5. Before you write that something does not exist, search the record for it, INDEX included (`index:WORDS`).
170	6. Decide whose choice it is, by "The choices that are yours" above.
171	7. Record each defect that you found as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says. If you make the choice and repair the defect, that is its item 1. If the question stays open, it is its item 3. Record a finding that is not a defect, such as a fact about the original tree, as `records.md`, "Writing to the record", says.
172	8. If your brief does not let you edit the ledger, put the ledger row in your report:
173	   1. Write the row in a file, in the form that `records.md` gives for a new row.
174	   2. Run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py check --rows FILE`. It counts the `?` in the number cell as a broken rule. Correct the row until the check names no other rule.
175	   3. Copy the row into your report.
176	9. If the question touches a passage of the specification, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
177	10. If the choice is yours, make it. Report it as a decision.
178	11. If the choice is the curator's, report it as a decision not taken. Give these:
179	    - the question;
180	    - each source, and its date ("Weighing the sources" above says what else to note);
181	    - each possible solution, and what it changes;
182	    - which solution keeps the current behaviour.
183	12. If you cannot get some evidence in your task, say in your report what is missing and how to get it.
184	# Committing and pushing
185	
186	**scratch**
187	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
188	
189	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
190	
191	## What to commit
192	
193	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
194	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
195	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
196	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
197	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
198	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
199	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
200	
201	## How to commit
202	
203	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
204	
205	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
206	
207	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
208	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
209	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
210	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
211	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
212	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
213	
214	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
215	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
216	
217	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
218	
219	## Pushing
220	
221	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
222	
223	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
224	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
225	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
226	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
227	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
228	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
229	
230	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
231	
232	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
233	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
234	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
235	# Setting up, building, the caches, and what to rebuild
236	
237	**tree**
238	: Checkout of the repository: the main checkout or a worktree. In a command, `<tree>` is the tree that you work in: the one that your brief names, else the one that your session starts in.
239	
240	**library order**
241	: Five compiles that build the compiled path's library into the caches.
242	
243	**DSL grammar**
244	: `grammar` declaration in an api, which adds syntax for a domain-specific language.
245	
246	**parser directory**
247	: New `fortress<random>rats` folder of 5.8 MB, in which a program that imports a DSL grammar gets a Rats! parser generated when it runs. The run makes it in its JVM's temporary directory and never deletes it.
248	
249	## Setting up each call
250	
251	Start every Bash call with these lines. They put you at the tree's root, where this skill's commands start unless they `cd`:
252	
253	    cd <tree> && mkdir -p tmp
254	    export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64 PATH=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64/bin:$PATH
255	    export FORTRESS_HOME=$PWD FORTRESS_THREADS=1 TMPDIR=$PWD/tmp JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"
256	    unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
257	
258	- If `/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64` or `ant` is missing, run `apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y openjdk-25-jdk-headless ant` first.
259	- `bin/fortress` takes `FORTRESS_HOME` from the shell whenever it is set. If it names another tree, you run that tree's code. Check it with `echo $FORTRESS_HOME`.
260	- `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` is unset, because the proxy's trust-store flags in it break ant's JVM forks.
261	
262	The lines give the settings of `explorations/experiment/env.sh`, with two differences:
263	
264	- The JVM's temporary directory is your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
265	- They leave out env.sh's removal of old parser directories in `/tmp`, because your runs put theirs in your tree's `tmp/` (below).
266	
267	If your brief tells you to run `source env.sh` and then to point `TMPDIR` and `JAVA_FLAGS` at `tmp/`, use the lines above. They do the same.
268	
269	The library and microGPT import no DSL grammar, and of the gated tests only `ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ForUse.fss` does. The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under `explorations/apl/`.
270	
271	With the lines above, your runs that import a DSL grammar put their parser directories in `<tree>/tmp/`. Hundreds of them once filled the disk allowance. So:
272	
273	- When no run of yours is live, remove yours: `rm -rf <tree>/tmp/fortress*rats`.
274	- Before a long run, check `df -h /`. How to read it: the `cloud-container` skill.
275	
276	## Two layers of code
277	
278	The repository holds two layers of code. Different tools build them, at different times, so "compile" means a different thing in each layer.
279	
280	The implementation is the parser, walk, the compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime. It is the Java and Scala under `ProjectFortress/src/`, with the parser grammars (`parser/*.rats`) and the syntax tree generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`. `ant compileAll` builds it into `ProjectFortress/build/` ("Building", below). `ant compile` is another name for it.
281	
282	The Fortress code is the library, the tests and the programs: the `.fss` and `.fsi` files. The `fortress` commands run the phases on it and keep the results in the caches:
283	
284	- Walk runs the phases on each component that a run needs. It needs no `fortress compile`.
285	- `fortress compile` writes a component's jar. It is for the compiled path's components only: the compiler's library, compiled tests and compiled programs.
286	- `fortress run` compiles no Fortress source.
287	- A command reuses an entry if no source that the entry depends on is newer than the entry: its own source, and the `.fsi` files of the apis that it imports, at any depth.
288	
289	An edit makes stale what was built from it:
290	
291	- Java or Scala: the classes in `ProjectFortress/build/`. Run `ant compileAll`. The cache entries that the edited code wrote are stale too, and no entry notices it: an entry is compared with its sources, never with the implementation. For example, after a change to a native helper's signature, its old wrapper stays in `nativewrapper_cache/`, and the run links the old signature. For this reason, the build deletes the caches when the implementation changes ("Building").
292	- A parser grammar: the generated parser, and every entry that it parsed. Run `ant compileAll`.
293	- A `.fss` or `.fsi` file of the library: the entries of that component, and after an `.fsi` edit, the entries of every component that imports the api. Walk analyses them again by itself. A component of the compiler's library needs a compile, or the library order ("After an edit of the library").
294	- A test or a program: its own entries. Walk and the harness analyse a walk test again by themselves. Compile a compiled test or program again, or let the harness do it.
295	
296	## The caches
297	
298	All the caches are gitignored. A caches folder also holds:
299	
300	- `environment_cache/`: another cache of walk's.
301	- `nativewrapper_cache/`: the wrappers for the Java classes that an api imports with `import java`.
302	- `global.map`: the linker's saved state, an empty map in practice. If it is missing, the linker writes an empty one, also in a private caches folder.
303	- `implementation.stamp`: the stamp of the build that the caches belong to ("Building", below).
304	
305	Only these runs read `default_repository/caches`: `fortress compile`, `fortress run`, `fortress junit` (and `junit.sh`), `ant testOnly`, and a direct walk run. These runs use private caches (`-Dfortress.caches` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`), and need neither the library order nor warm caches: `harness-one.sh`, the gate's ladder regression (`gate.md`) and both ant suites. `harness-one.sh` keeps its private cache beside its scratch folder between calls (`tests-running.md`).
306	
307	## The library order
308	
309	The first of its compiles, `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, holds the top type `Any`, which both libraries share. The other four are the compiler's own. All five take about 100 to 110 s after `ant compileAll`.
310	
311	Run it only when the caches lack the library's jars, or hold stale ones:
312	
313	- after a build that printed `Caches <tree>/default_repository/caches started again, empty`, and in a tree whose caches are empty;
314	- after an edit of a library `.fsi` that the section "After an edit of the library" names.
315	
316	Otherwise the jars are in place, and a compiled test or program needs no library order. The five commands:
317	
318	    cd ProjectFortress
319	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss            # 17 s
320	    ../bin/fortress compile LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss    # 63 s
321	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss        # 27 s
322	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss        # 2 s
323	    ../bin/fortress compile ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss         # 2 s
324	
325	Before the first compiled run, check that `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/` holds five jars: `fortress.AnyType.jar`, `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`, `fortress.CompilerLibrary.jar`, `fortress.CompilerAlgebra.jar` and `CompilerSystem.jar`, which has no prefix. Sometimes all five compiles exit 0 and a jar is missing. The cause is not known.
326	
327	- If a jar is missing, run the five commands again. Once, this made the jars.
328	- If a jar is still missing, report it as a defect. Quote the commands, their exit codes and the folder's listing.
329	- Keep the caches in this case too. Once, emptying them made the jars, but a deletion hides the cause.
330	
331	## Name resolution
332	
333	- `fortress.source.path` searches `.` (the current directory) first, then `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin`, `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/test_library`. The first `Foo.fsi` or `Foo.fss` that it finds wins. So a file in the directory that you run from hides the library's file of the same name.
334	- A component's file name without `.fss` must be the component's name.
335	- If both libraries use one api name, one of them breaks. For this reason, the compiler's apis have the `Compiler` prefix.
336	- The top-level `CompilerLibrary/` holds `.fsi`-only stubs, not `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss`. `lib/` holds Fortress sources, not jars.
337	- If paths behave wrongly, read `repository/ProjectProperties.java`. It resolves `FORTRESS_HOME`, `BASEDIR` and the cache paths.
338	
339	## Building
340	
341	Run `ant compileAll` from the tree's root. It is the only build: `ProjectFortress/build.xml` is a stub.
342	
343	- It makes the parser and the syntax tree again only if their sources changed.
344	- javac compiles only the changed Java files and the files that depend on them. scalac runs only if its inputs changed, and then compiles every Scala file.
345	- It decides by a stamp whether it deletes the caches. `ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp` is a hash of the built implementation, and each caches folder holds the stamp of the build that filled it. At its end, the build keeps `default_repository/caches` if its stamp equals the new one, and empties it if not. It does not touch a private caches folder. It prints `Caches <folder> kept` or `Caches <folder> started again, empty`. The comment "The caches and the implementation" in `build.xml` gives the rule.
346	- `ant cleanCache` deletes the caches, whatever their stamp.
347	- With nothing changed, it takes about 4 s. After an edit, it takes about 25 to 60 s on an idle machine, scalac about 19 s of it, and about 50 to 80 s on a new or cleaned tree. While other agents build, it takes up to about 140 s.
348	- After a build that started the caches again, yours or a test target's, run the library order before the next compiled run. So each edit of Java or Scala costs about 2 to 3 minutes before a compiled run: the build, then the library order.
349	- If it fails, fix the error and run the same command again. Clear nothing by hand.
350	
351	## After an edit of the library
352	
353	The compiled path sees an edit of its library only when you compile the edited component itself. Compiling your own program never recompiles the library under it.
354	
355	- If you edited the `.fss` of one of the five library components, and not its `.fsi`: run `fortress compile` on that component only. Programs need no recompile.
356	- If you edited the `.fsi` of AnyType, CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary or CompilerAlgebra: run the whole library order. Every api depends on these four.
357	- If you edited `CompilerSystem.fsi`: compile CompilerSystem only.
358	- If you edited any other file of `Library/` or `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: it is walk's library. Do nothing: walk reads it again, and compiled programs do not link it yet.
359	
360	## Symptoms of a skipped step
361	
362	If you skip the step for your edit, the run shows it:
363	
364	- After an edit of a body, the run uses the old code and gives no warning.
365	- After an edit of an api, the run stops with `NoSuchMethodError` or `NoClassDefFoundError` on a library member. Examples: `fortress.CompilerBuiltin.println`, `coerce_ZZ32`, `fortress/CompilerLibrary$GeneratorZZ32`. The run found no library jar and used the bootstrap stubs: old class files of the compiler's library that the build compiles from `ProjectFortress/src/fortress/` into `ProjectFortress/build/fortress/`.
366	
367	If you see either, do the step now: recompile the component, or run the library order. Do not delete the caches to fix it. A deletion works only because it repeats the library order and every analysis from cold. If something else looks like a stale cache, find its cause before you delete anything.
368	
369	Two messages look like a skipped step, but usually show a defect:
370	
371	- A `NoSuchMethodError` on a method of your own program, often with a mangled name such as `\=tag?1??Arrow...`, is a defect of the compiled path. Record it (`tests-writing.md`).
372	- "Unable to read serialized data for X, recommend you delete the Fortress bytecode cache and relink" is usually a defect of the code generator. Search the gap ledger for the message. Run the library order only if X is a member of a `Compiler*` or `AnyType` component. Keep the caches, whatever the message advises.
373	
374	Two more facts help you read a run:
375	
376	- A `fortress compile` of a source that did not change, and whose jar exists, writes nothing and exits 0.
377	- A library compile that failed or was killed wrote nothing, or only its jar. Programs link the old jar with no warning until you fix the error and compile that component again.
378

3	# The switch-over rehearsed by brute force
4	
5	The question: what stands between today's tree (`832f7d0d91`) and a program that compiles to bytecode and runs against the interpreter's library (P-37, P-33)? The method: switch a scratch tree's compiled path onto that library by the smallest change, then push, hacking past each wall, and record the walls in the order met. A hack is marked as one in the patch (`SWITCH HACK`), and the patch is not a design.
6	
7	Machine: nproc 4, Intel Xeon Processor @ 2.30GHz, OpenJDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`. Other sessions share the machine.
8	
9	How the runs were made: the edited Java and Scala classes compiled into a scratch folder put first on the class path (the `fortress-repo` skill's `compiler.md`, "Testing an edit here"), with a private caches folder that started empty; one `ant compileAll` after the run-time classes changed.
10	
11	## 1. The switch itself

POSITIONS.md:41

So the library's numbers are flat, as the team (Chase, Ryu, Maessen and Allen) flattened the compiler prelude in 2009 and 2010. The fixed widths, `ZZ`, `QQ` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`, each with its own algebra, and `Number` has no catch-all operators. Why: the flattened prelude is the team's last record of the Fortress way, and its route leads to the POPL 2019 paper, which keeps the rule. POSITIONS.md:110
- P-84 **On the compiled path, the array of every number type is to be stored unboxed, in a Java array of its primitive type, and every array is to have the most efficient store that its element type allows; arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** `RR64` goes in a `double[]`, `ZZ32` in an `int[]`, and so on, for each number type that has a Java primitive type; `RR64`'s `double[]`, the model's, is the first case. Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, on extending the library in its own way). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67).
